title: He Broke the 100m Record Three Times in Two Days. Modi Opened Mann Ki Baat With His Name.
excerpt: Gurindervir Singh's 10.09 seconds and Vishal TK's sub-45 quarter-mile made Ranchi the birthplace of a new era in Indian sprinting. The PM took notice.
body:
On a warm May evening at the Birsa Munda Stadium in Ranchi, Indian sprinting crossed two thresholds it had been chasing for a generation.

In the space of a few minutes on May 23, two athletes wrote their names into the record books at the 29th National Senior Athletics Federation Cup. Gurindervir Singh ran the 100 metres in 10.09 seconds. Vishal TK ran the 400 metres in 44.98 seconds. Both are national records. Both shattered barriers that Indian athletics had been pushing against for decades.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated the achievement on his Mann Ki Baat programme on Sunday, opening the broadcast by highlighting India's sprint breakthroughs at the National Senior Athletics Championships. The national record in the 100 metres, he noted, had been broken three times in two days.

## The Fastest Indian in History

The 100-metre final in Ranchi was the climax of one of the most dramatic rivalries in Indian track and field.

Gurindervir Singh, a 25-year-old Petty Officer in the Indian Navy from Jalandhar, Punjab, had set the stage the previous evening. In the semi-finals on May 22, he ran 10.17 seconds to break the existing national record of 10.18 held by Animesh Kujur of Odisha. Within five minutes, in the very next heat, Kujur responded with 10.15 seconds and seized the record right back.

Two national records, traded between two athletes, in the same evening.

Twenty-four hours later, in the final, Gurindervir settled the argument. Running from lane four with a legal tailwind of +0.3 metres per second, he drove hard through the middle phase and crossed the line in 10.09 seconds — the first Indian to breach the 10.10-second barrier. He finished nearly two feet ahead of Kujur, who clocked 10.20 in second place. Pranav Gurav took bronze in 10.29.

"This record is to prove that I'm not finished and still have power in my legs," Gurindervir said afterwards.

His coach, James Hillier, the British sprint specialist who heads the Reliance Foundation programme, was measured but optimistic. "He is learning to execute the plans in the races, and his performance graph is getting better," Hillier said, adding he expected further improvement ahead of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in July.

The 10.09 comfortably clears the Athletics Federation of India's Commonwealth Games entry standard of 10.16 seconds. It is currently the second-fastest time in Asia this season, behind only Japanese teenager Fukuto Komuro's 10.08.

## India's First Sub-45 Man

Minutes after Gurindervir's record, the Birsa Munda scoreboard lit up again.

Vishal TK, a 22-year-old from Jolarpettai in Tamil Nadu's Tirupattur district, ran the 400 metres final in 44.98 seconds — making him the first Indian man to officially break the 45-second barrier over one lap. The bib he held up to the camera read "44 COMING HOME."

Vishal's trajectory defies convention. Until two years ago, he was a 100-metre and 200-metre sprinter who had never made a national mark. His coach at the time, Sreenivasan Ramaiah, suggested he move up to the quarter-mile. In April 2024 his personal best stood at 46.77 seconds. At one national meet that year, he finished last in his race.

By August 2025, training under Jamaican coach Jason Dawson at the National Centre of Excellence in Thiruvananthapuram, he had broken Muhammed Anas Yahiya's six-year-old national record with 45.12 seconds. In Ranchi, he obliterated his own mark.

Rajesh Ramesh finished second in 45.31 seconds, while Jay Kumar took bronze in 45.47 — both inside the previous meet record. The top three finishers in the same race all ran faster than a mark that had stood since 2016.

There is a cruel footnote: the AFI's Commonwealth Games qualifying time for the 400 metres is 44.96 seconds. Vishal missed it by two-hundredths of a second. Whether selectors pick him on discretion will be a conversation for the coming days. The 44.98 itself, however, is permanent.

## A Shift, Not a Spike

What happened at Ranchi is not isolated brilliance. It is the visible result of a structural shift in Indian sprinting that has been building since 2024.

The 100-metre national record has now been broken five times in 14 months, after standing untouched for a quarter of a century. Three sprinters — Gurindervir, Animesh, and Manikanta Hoblidhar — have all run faster than 10.20 in that span. All three train within the Reliance Foundation sprint programme under international coaches who have been given multiple seasons to develop young Indian sprinters in a structured way.

The 400 metres has seen a parallel revolution. Five Indian men are now consistently running sub-46 seconds, a depth that did not exist even two years ago.

For the Indian diaspora, these breakthroughs carry a particular resonance. For decades, the popular assumption — in India and abroad — was that Indian athletes were not built for sprinting. Cricket dominated the national conversation, and athletics existed in its shadow. What Ranchi demonstrated is that with the right coaching infrastructure, private investment, and a critical mass of athletes pushing each other, that narrative can change fast.

The Commonwealth Games in Glasgow begin on July 23. For the first time in living memory, Indian sprint events are something to actually watch — not politely hope about.
